name: The Bodhi Tree of Pearl's Hill

location.address: Pearl's Hill City Park, hilltop near the Service Reservoir gate, Singapore

access: Free, public park (Pearl's Hill City Park), no gates or opening hours found
transport: Short walk (roughly 5-10 minutes, uphill) from Outram Park MRT station (East-West/North-East/Thomson-East Coast lines)
verify_notes: NParks Heritage Tree register HT 2001-18: girth 6.34m at 1.3m height, height 16.9m. Second source (Little Day Out, a Singapore lifestyle/travel site) independently names 'the heritage Bodhi Tree found near the summit' of Pearl's Hill City Park as one of the park's notable features. No age given by NParks; leave empty rather than guess. IMPORTANT: do not confuse with the Bodhi Tree at Jin Long Si Temple, a different, much more widely covered tree (subject of a 'visitors flock to save revered Bodhi Tree' news story and a preserved-by-tender-condition redevelopment saga); that is a different individual, not this one, and none of that story belongs in this tree's copy. Pearl's Hill itself has real history: named for Captain James Pearl (commander of the Indiana, the ship that brought Raffles to Singapore in 1819), former site of Tan Tock Seng's original Chinese Paupers' Hospital and Singapore's first prison. Ficus religiosa is the species under which the Buddha is traditionally said to have attained enlightenment, sacred to both Buddhists and Hindus. Good writer hook: a sacred fig on a hill named for the ship's captain who brought Raffles ashore, growing over the site of Singapore's first prison and its first pauper's hospital.

name: The Banyan of Tiong Bahru Park
age_estimate: under 60 years (planted after the park opened in 1967)
access: Free, public park, no gates or opening hours found
transport: Roughly 10-15 minute walk from Tiong Bahru or Redhill MRT station
verify_notes: NParks Heritage Tree register HT 2013-204: girth 22.8m at 1.3m height (huge), height 18.4m. NParks' own text is explicit and important: 'Tiong Bahru Park was developed in 1967. This Tree was planted thereafter,' so despite the enormous girth this is NOT an old tree by this project's usual standard, well under 60 years as of 2026. FLAG THIS FOR THE WRITER: a general web search for 'Tiong Bahru banyan trees' surfaces claims of 'ancient banyan trees over 100 years old' in the wider Tiong Bahru area, but that describes different specimens elsewhere in the neighbourhood (likely near the old Kampong Tiong Bahru), not this specific registered park tree; do not let the two blend into one claim. What makes this one worth the walk is the girth/age mismatch itself: a banyan can reach a girth most trees need centuries for within a few decades, because its aerial prop roots fuse into the trunk and thicken it fast. Ficus benghalensis is sacred to Hindus (roots as Brahma's abode, trunk as Vishnu's, branches as Shankar's, per the register's own text). Second source: Wikipedia's Tiong Bahru Park page (development history, 1967 opening, corroborates NParks' own planting-date note). Good writer hook: a fig with the girth of a giant and the age of a Baby Boomer, whose speed is the story rather than its years.

name: The Earpod Tree of Fort Canning

location.address: Fort Canning Park, between the Fort Wall and Hotel Fort Canning, Singapore

transport: 8-10 minute walk from Fort Canning MRT station (Downtown Line)
verify_notes: NParks Heritage Tree register HT 2001-11: girth 5.94m at 1.3m height, height 17.9m, located 'along path behind the Fort Wall and The Legends'. Second source: NParks' own current Fort Canning Park DIY walking-trail PDF (a separate curated document, not the register page) lists this same tree as stop 1, 'Between Fort Wall and Hotel Fort Canning' (The Legends and Hotel Fort Canning are the same building complex), with no indication of any damage. UNRESOLVED FLAG, do not smooth over: a travel blog (travelertina.blog, Nov 2025) separately describes 'a fallen earpod tree (Enterolobium cyclocarpum)... that toppled over during a 2014 storm but continues to grow, supporting orchids, ferns and other epiphytes' in Fort Canning Park, with no location detail given beyond 'the park'. It is not confirmed whether this is the SAME tree as HT 2001-11 or a different, unregistered Earpod tree elsewhere in the park; the register's own current data (girth/height figures, last updated 2025-08-18) and the official current DIY trail brochure both describe HT 2001-11 in ordinary upright terms with no mention of a fall. Ships flagged rather than blocked because the weight of the more current, more specific evidence (register + official trail guide, both current) says standing; a writer or later pass should look at an actual photo before finalising copy, and phrase around the toppled-tree claim rather than assert either way if uncertain. Species notes: native to tropical dry forest from Mexico to Venezuela, one of the largest trees of that habitat (up to 40m/3m diameter in the wild), older specimens develop surface roots that crack nearby paving; seed pods are distinctively ear-shaped, giving the common name (also called devil's ear or elephant-ear tree).
